opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it starts with being very clear about what the ultimate goal is, even if it seems almost impossibly ambitious. For me, from a very young age, that was understanding intelligence and then using it to help us understand the universe around us. But you can't just go straight at something like that. You have to break it down.

So what I try to do is work backwards from the dream. You ask: what are the stepping stones? What's the next thing that, if we solved it, would be both meaningful in itself and would move us measurably closer to the big goal? That's partly why games were so useful for us early on at DeepMind. They're a perfect proving ground. They have clear objectives, you can measure progress unambiguously, and you can generate as much data as you like. So Atari, then Go with AlphaGo, those weren't the end goal. They were milestones that told us whether our general learning approaches were actually working.

Then there's the question of choosing which scientific problems to go after. I look for a few things. First, is it a root node problem, something that, if you crack it, unlocks a whole tree of downstream discoveries? Protein folding was like that. Second, is there a clear objective function, some metric you can hill-climb against? Third, is there enough data, or a way to generate it, say through simulation? If a problem ticks those boxes, it's often ripe for AI right now.

And timing matters enormously. There's this idea I sometimes talk about of being five years ahead, not fifty. If you're too early, the tools and the compute aren't there and you just bang your head against a wall. So you have to have this dual mindset: be incredibly ambitious about the long-term vision but very pragmatic and rigorous about what's actually tractable today.

The last piece is the people and the culture. I've always tried to blend the best of academia, that deep scientific rigor and long-term thinking, with the focus and energy of a startup. You bring together brilliant people from many different disciplines, give them a really clear mission, and make sure they can move quickly. When you get that combination right, things that looked like science fiction a decade ago start becoming engineering problems. And that's always the moment that's most exciting to me.

r001.rationale: It says the next stepping stone should be “meaningful in itself” while also moving measurably toward the larger goal.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing is to be honest with yourself about the difference between a dream and a project. The dream, for me, has always been the same since I was a kid, really: can we build a system that can learn to solve any problem, and then use that to help us understand the universe? That's the north star. But you can't work on that directly on a Monday morning. It's too big, too vague. You'd just stare at it.

So what we've always done at DeepMind is try to find the right intermediate problem. And I think there's actually a bit of an art to choosing it. The problem needs to be hard enough that if you solve it, you've genuinely learned something new, something that generalizes. But it also needs to be tractable within a reasonable horizon, maybe three to five years, so that a team can actually stay motivated and you can tell whether you're making progress. Games were perfect for that early on. Go was a fantastic example. Everyone said it was a decade or more away, it had this huge search space, it required something like intuition. But it also had a crisp objective, you could run millions of simulations, and you knew unambiguously whether you'd won or lost. That clarity is incredibly valuable.

Then protein folding was the same kind of thing but in science. It had been an open problem for fifty years, there was a well-defined benchmark in CASP that the community already trusted, and critically, there was a lot of good data. So when I looked at it, I thought, this has the shape of something our methods could crack, and if we crack it, it matters enormously beyond the problem itself.

The other thing I'd say is that you have to resist the temptation to pick problems that are just impressive-looking. The question I always ask is: if we succeed at this, what does it unlock? Does it put us one rung further up the ladder towards the real goal, or is it a dead end that happens to look good? And conversely, you have to be willing to pick things that seem almost unreasonably ambitious, because I actually think the biggest risk is being too conservative. The great thing about these moonshot-type problems is they attract the best people, and the best people want to work on things that might not work.

And then finally, I'd say it's about building the right kind of organization around it. A lot of this came from thinking about how the great labs of the past worked, places like Bell Labs or the early Cambridge biology labs. You need a mix of blue-sky thinking and real engineering discipline. Setting a hard deadline, having a measurable goal, and then giving a brilliant multidisciplinary team the freedom to figure out how to get there. That combination, that's what I've always found turns the dream into something you can actually do.

r001.rationale: The response says an intermediate problem should teach something new and generalizable, and uses protein folding as an example that matters beyond solving the problem itself.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to have a very ambitious long-term vision, but then be quite pragmatic about the steps that get you there. You can’t just say, ‘We’re going to solve intelligence,’ and expect that to tell you what to work on on Monday morning.

You have to break it down into questions you can actually test. What capability is missing? What experiment would tell us whether our approach is right? And can we find a problem that’s challenging enough to force a new idea, but constrained enough that we can measure progress?

Games are a good example of that. They give you a clear objective and a way to evaluate the system, while still requiring quite sophisticated learning and planning. But you have to keep asking whether what you’re developing will generalize beyond that particular game.

So there’s this constant movement between the big picture and the next experiment. The dream gives you direction, but the experimental results have to determine your next step—even when they’re telling you something you didn’t want to hear.

r001.rationale: The response describes breaking the goal into testable, measurable steps, but does not say those intermediate steps should have value in their own right.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to have a very ambitious long-term vision, but then work backwards from it. What would have to be true for us to get there? What are the major obstacles, and which of those can we actually make progress on today?

Then you need to find a concrete problem that captures something essential about that bigger ambition, but where you can run experiments and measure whether your ideas are working. Games were useful for us in that way: clear objectives, clear rules, and an opportunity to test learning and planning.

There’s a balance, though. If you only pursue the next achievable milestone, you can lose sight of the big question. And if you only think about the big question, you may never build anything. You need that connection between the two—and the willingness to change your route when the experiments tell you you’re wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says intermediate problems should connect to the larger ambition and allow experiments, but does not state that those steps should have value in their own right.
